questions.question: Is composition commutative, that is, does $g\circ f=f\circ g$ in general?
questions.explanation: Composition is generally noncommutative. For $f(x)=x+1$, $g(x)=2x$, one gets $g\circ f=2x+2$ but $f\circ g=2x+1$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: The explicit counterexample gives unequal composites.
Equality can occur even when $f\ne g$, such as two compatible identity-like maps; it is not an iff condition.
The linear/affine example above already shows that linear-type formulas need not commute.

questions.question: For $f\colon X\to Y$, what is $f\circ \mathrm{id}_X$?
questions.explanation: The identity acts first and returns $x$, so $(f\circ\mathrm{id}_X)(x)=f(x)$ for every $x\in X$.

questions.question: If $f$ and $g$ are bijections, what is $(g\circ f)^{-1}$?
questions.explanation: To undo $g\circ f$, reverse the order: $f^{-1}\circ g^{-1}\circ g\circ f=\mathrm{id}$. Thus $(g\circ f)^{-1}=f^{-1}\circ g^{-1}$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

Likewise $g\circ f$ is the map being inverted, not its inverse.
